narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Sipi Tau, penned by King Taufaʻahau Tupou IV in 1994, is a fierce war dance chant performed by Tonga's rugby teams to intimidate opponents.
This is Sipi Tau. 19th century origins; 1994 formal rugby adaptation.

Title card: Sipi Tau · Tonga · 19th century origins; 1994 formal rugby adaptation

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Sipi Tau originates from the traditional Kailao war dance of Wallis and Futuna, which Tonga annexed in the 19th century.
Originally, Tongan war dances did not involve singing, as silence was valued in battle.
The Kailao is a fierce dance performed with clubs and percussion, emulating combat.
on_screen: Map: Tonga · Oceania
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Sipi Tau is performed before rugby union and league matches by Tonga's national teams as a war-cry and challenge to opponents.
It symbolizes warrior spirit, unity, and national pride.
It is not a sacred dance but a cultural expression meant to intimidate and inspire.

music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Sipi Tau (Tonga). New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.

wardrobe.policy: neutral dress with a respectful nod (palette and fabric only): the sources describe sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire, or the dance is sacred

visual_brief.costume_notes: The Kailao dance involves men bearing stylized clubs called pate kailao and is performed at public and private ceremonies. The Sipi Tau, performed by rugby teams, is done in sports uniforms on the field before matches. The setting is a stadium or rugby pitch, and the performance is a public display of cultural identity and intimidation.
visual_brief.setting_notes: The Sipi Tau is performed before rugby union and league matches by Tonga's national teams as a war-cry and challenge to opponents. It symbolizes warrior spirit, unity, and national pride. It is not a sacred dance but a cultural expression meant to intimidate and inspire. The Kailao is performed at ceremonies and showcases discipline and combat skills.
